newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica oil sector told to empower blacks.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica oil sector told to empower blacks.

text.p: South Africa's white-controlled oil industry has been sent a strong message to prepare for greater black participation and ownership.
The message came in the maiden budget speech of South Africa's first black minister for minerals and energy, Penuell Maduna.
Although short on detail, Maduna's speech spelled out the need to ensure greater black ownership.
Maduna has kept a relatively low profile since he was appointed in July 1996 to take over from Pik Botha, whose National Party had left President Nelson Mandela's government of national unity.
Maduna's first budget speech on May 21 was widely regarded as a major opportunity to learn of the policies of Maduna and his new team of black staff and advisers.

The industry was also hoping for some firm hint on when Maduna would finalise his new policy on regulation of the industry, and in particular on the granting of a wholesale margin increase which has been due since the beginning of 1996.

Instead, it had to be satisfied with assurances that Maduna knew that finalising the "rules of the game" was urgent given the investment decisions that had to be made soon to expand refinery capacity to meet growing demand.

But Maduna's main concern, both in his speech and in a separate media briefing, was the need to involve more blacks in the oil industry, which he saw as a way for government to deliver on its promises to distribute ownership and wealth.
He had ruffled a few feathers a week before by mentioning in a speech that he was considering the establishment of a national oil company to achieve black involvement.

He said he could not understand what the fuss was all about as what he was considering was the restructuring of the state-owned Central Energy Fund and its string of oil storage and production subsidiaries.
The new company could be listed, as and when appropriate, on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange with government retaining majority control.

This would provide a vehicle for black involvement in the industry while adding value to state oil assets, which include an offshore oilfield, oil-from-gas producer Mossgas and three pipelines running from Durban to Gauteng.
South African Petroleum Industry Association (SAPIA) director Colin McClelland told Reuters the industry was aware of and supported the need for greater black involvement.
"We welcome further black advancement in the industry and it is refreshing to see government looking at its assets and wanting to add value to them while assisting black empowerment," he said.
"But the playing fields should be level for all investors, other than things constitutionally done to assist blacks."

Analysts said that state-owned oil exploration company Soekor, which has already sold 20 percent of its first oil field to Energy Africa Ltd, might be expected to sell off some shares to black companies.
The major oil companies -- Shell South Africa Ltd., BP, Total SA, Engen Ltd. and Caltex -- were unlikely to be happy if the government favoured the state oil company over and above the others.

"Another danger would be if the government made decisions about issues such as margin increases based purely on the state oil company's needs and not the best interests of the economy," said one analyst.

South Africa's oil industry was swathed in secrecy during the apartheid years, when international oil sanctions forced the apartheid government to establish the Central Energy Fund to buy oil, mainly from Iran, and build up massive stocks at a special tank farm at Sldanha Bay and in disused coal mines in the interior.

It also poured billions of dollars into oil-from-coal producer Sasol Ltd., which has since been partially privatised and listed on the Johannesburg stock exchange, and oil-from-gas producer Mossgas, which has been described as a white elephant because of limited gas reserves.
Both still receive state subsidies and attempts to sell Mossgas have been unsuccessful.

A clutch of companies in the energy sector have been established by black South Africans in recent years, notably Naledi and AfricOil, but their actual involvement in the industry has been limited to running service stations.
